title: 1 Kings 2:13–25
context: Adonijah the son of Haggith comes to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. She asks, “Do you come peaceably?” and he says that he does. He then asks her to hear him, recalls that the kingdom had been his expectation, and grants that it has been turned and has become his brother’s, “for it was his from the LORD.” He asks one petition: that she speak to Solomon so that Abishag the Shunammite may be given to him as wife. Bathsheba agrees and goes in. Solomon rises to meet her, bows, and seats her on his right hand. She calls the request “one small petition” When she names it—“Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife”—Solomon answers, “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.” That is how the text frames the request: Solomon treats it as tied to a claim on the throne, and that is the common reading of his judgment. The narrator does not separately state Adonijah’s inner motive, and the notes should not add anything about Abishag beyond the petition itself and what was already said in chapter 1. Solomon swears by the LORD, who has established him on David’s throne and made him a house as he promised, that Adonijah shall be put to death that day. He sends Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, “and he fell on him, so that he died.” Both traditions report the death as the narrator gives it, without sensationalizing it and without inventing a party dispute over the ethics of royal succession.

verses.text: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. She said, “Do you come peaceably?” He said, “Peaceably.
verses.arminianNotes:
Adonijah the son of Haggith comes to Bathsheba, and she asks, “Do you come peaceably?” He said, “Peaceably.” The greeting is about peace, and her question shows that peace is not assumed.

Arminian readers hear a cautious meeting. Bathsheba does not grant the visit a purpose until he speaks, and he begins by claiming a peaceable coming.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the question seriously. “Do you come peaceably?” is the first word, and his “Peaceably” is the first answer, not yet the petition.

Both traditions start from this exchange as it stands, without reading the later request back into the greeting as if it had already been spoken.

verses.text: He said moreover, I have something to tell you.” She said, “Say on.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He says he has something to tell her, and she answers, “Say on.” He asks to be heard, and she permits him to speak, still without knowing the petition.

Arminian readers hear a second approach after the claim of peace. He asks for a hearing, and she grants it, not yet the request itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise treat “Say on.” as her leave to continue. She has heard a request to listen, not yet the petition itself.

Both traditions take the line as the door to the request, not as the request itself.

verses.text: He said, “You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign. However, the kingdom is turned around, and has become my brother’s; for it was his from the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
He said, “You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign. However, the kingdom is turned around, and has become my brother’s; for it was his from the LORD.” He admits, in the same breath, both his own earlier expectation and the LORD’s giving of the kingdom to Solomon.

Arminian readers hear a real concession: “for it was his from the LORD.” Adonijah says the turn of the kingdom was the LORD’s, even as he still remembers that he had looked to reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that same clause. The kingdom “has become my brother’s; for it was his from the LORD.” That admission will sit beside the petition that follows.

Both traditions let him speak both parts. They do not yet decide the request; they note that he himself has said the throne was Solomon’s from the LORD.

verses.text: Now I ask one petition of you. Don’t deny me.” She said to him, “Say on.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now I ask one petition of you. Don’t deny me.” She said, “Say on.” He still has not named the thing he wants; he asks her not to refuse him, and she again tells him to speak.

Arminian readers hear the pressure of the plea before its content. He asks for an answer of yes, and she has not yet heard what the petition is.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the verse in its place. “Don’t deny me.” is a request for her consent, still unspecific, and “Say on.” is her second permission to speak.

Both traditions wait with her for the name of the petition in the next verse.

verses.text: He said, “Please speak to Solomon the king (for he will not tell you ‘no’), that he give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He said, “Please speak to Solomon the king (for he will not tell you ‘no’), that he give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife.” This is the petition: Abishag is to be given to him as wife, and he thinks Bathsheba’s word will not be refused.

Arminian readers keep the request inside those words. He asks for Abishag as wife. The verse does not describe her, and it does not add intimacy or motive beyond the asking. What the request means for the throne is taken up when Solomon answers it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to say more about Abishag than the petition states. The earlier notice that the king did not know her intimately remains the narrator’s limit from chapter 1.

Both traditions record the request soberly and wait for Solomon’s reading of it, which the text itself will soon supply.

verses.text: Bathsheba said, “All right. I will speak for you to the king.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Bathsheba said, “All right. I will speak for you to the king.” She agrees to carry the petition. The narrator does not say whether she sees in it what Solomon will see.

Arminian readers hear a real consent to speak, not yet a consent to the politics Solomon will name. She says she will speak for him, and the next verses show her doing so.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to invent her inner reading. “All right. I will speak for you to the king.” is what she says, and she goes.

Both traditions treat her agreement as the narrative gives it, without deciding for her why the petition seemed, or did not seem, small.

verses.text: Bathsheba therefore went to King Solomon, to speak to him for Adonijah. The king rose up to meet her and bowed himself to her, and sat down on his throne and caused a throne to be set for the king’s mother; and she sat on his right hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
She goes to King Solomon to speak for Adonijah. “The king rose up to meet her and bowed himself to her, and sat down on his throne and caused a throne to be set for the king’s mother; and she sat on his right hand.” The honor given to the king’s mother is public and formal.

Arminian readers hear genuine respect. Solomon rises, bows, and seats her at his right hand before he hears the petition.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same honor. A throne is set for the king’s mother, and she sits at his right hand.

Both traditions take the courtesy as real, and they do not read it as already granting the request she has come to make.

verses.text: Then she said, “I ask one small petition of you; don’t deny me.” The king said to her, “Ask on, my mother, for I will not deny you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Then she said, “I ask one small petition of you; don’t deny me.” The king said to her, “Ask on, my mother, for I will not deny you.” She calls the petition small, and he promises, in advance of hearing it, that he will not deny her.

Arminian readers hear the risk in that promise. He has not yet heard the content, and she has already named it small.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the two lines together: “one small petition” and “I will not deny you.” The next verse will test both.

Both traditions let the exchange stand. The honor of verse 19 continues in his address, “my mother,” just before the request is named.

verses.text: She said, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She said, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife.” The petition is now spoken in the throne room, in the same terms Adonijah used, with the added word that he is Solomon’s brother.

Arminian readers keep the sentence spare. She asks that Abishag be given as wife. Nothing is added about the woman, and nothing is added about a hidden plan that this verse does not state.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise report only the request as worded. “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife.” is the whole of her speech here.

Both traditions handle the line soberly and turn, with the narrative, to Solomon’s answer.

verses.text: King Solomon answered his mother, “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
King Solomon answered his mother, “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.” This is how the text frames the request. Solomon treats it as tied to a claim on the throne, names Adonijah as his elder brother, and joins Abiathar and Joab to the same danger.

Arminian readers take that framing as Solomon’s spoken judgment, and as the common reading of the scene. The narrator does not add a separate window into Adonijah’s heart, and the notes should not invent one.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to go beyond the king’s words. “Ask for him the kingdom also” is Solomon’s own account of what the petition means, and it is the common way the passage has been read.

Both traditions present that reading as the text’s framing, hedged as the common reading, not as a hidden motive freshly discovered in Abishag herself.

verses.text: Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, “God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, “God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life.” The petition, in Solomon’s oath, is a word against Adonijah’s life.

Arminian readers hear a solemn and public vow, not a whispered anger. Solomon binds himself by the LORD, and he treats the spoken request as fatal to the man who made it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the oath form. “God do so to me, and more also” introduces a sentence on the word Adonijah has spoken.

Both traditions report the vow as the narrator gives it. The sentence of death is completed in the next verse, and it is not to be sensationalized here.

verses.text: Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and set me on my father David’s throne, and who has made me a house as he promised, surely Adonijah shall be put to death today.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He continues, “Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and set me on my father David’s throne, and who has made me a house as he promised, surely Adonijah shall be put to death today.” The LORD’s establishing, the throne of David, and the promised house are the ground Solomon names, and the time is today.

Arminian readers hear him confess that the LORD has established him and kept a promise, and then name a sentence he will carry out that day. The confession and the sentence stand together in his mouth, without being turned into a party argument about succession ethics.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep both parts: the living LORD who has established Solomon and made him a house as he promised, and the sure word that Adonijah shall be put to death today.

Both traditions take the verse as Solomon’s sworn resolve, reported plainly, and as a claim that the promised house is already in the LORD’s hands.

verses.text: King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell on him, so that he died.
verses.arminianNotes:
“King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell on him, so that he died.” The narrator states the fact in a short clause. Benaiah is sent, he falls on Adonijah, and Adonijah dies.

Arminian readers let the sentence be as spare as it is. The death is reported, not described at length, and it should not be embellished or used to invent a fork over royal succession.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the same restraint. “he fell on him, so that he died” is the whole of the act as the book gives it.

Both traditions report the execution as the narrator gives it, without sensationalizing it, and they leave the ethical evaluations that readers may bring to the scene as differences that run inside both traditions, not as a required party contrast.
